newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia welcomes EU move, vows more reforms.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia welcomes EU move, vows more reforms.

text.p: Yugoslavia welcomed trade privileges granted by the European Union on Tuesday and said the deal would help it to speed up economic reforms.
But the EU warned that lack of democratic progress or backtracking from the Dayton peace agreement would lead to their withdrawal.

The trade benefits -- which include offering duty-free access and eliminating restrictions on imports into the EU of industrial products -- were needed to help the country's struggling economy, the EU said.

The Yugoslav Foreign Ministry said "the decision is an important step in the...development of comprehensive cooperation both in the interest of ... Yugoslavia and the European Union and its member states."

"(Yugoslavia) is convinced that the future will bring speedy development of overall relations with the European Union which should support innovation of former agreements and conclusion of new ones," it said in a statement.
Federal government members reacted with enthusiasm.

"This is really great news, even though it was expected. It is a recognition of positive changes in Yugoslavia by the EU ministers and we see their decision as support to continue with reforms," Yugoslavia's deputy prime minister, Danko Djunic, told Reuters.

"I hope that the EU move, by which it gave us some carrot but kept waiving a long, heavy stick, will be productive, because we shall speed up reforms, privatisation, liberalisation of our trade regime and development of the local financial market," Djunic said.

"The decision also has a great psychological importance both home and abroad and gives hope that Yugoslavia will be integrated and accepted as an equal member of the international community," Djunic added.
The deputy prime minister, in charge of overall economic reforms, said it was too early to estimate full effects of the granted trade benefits.

"Those privileges give us a chance to enter competition on the EU market on an equal footing. They will help Yugoslav export industries revive and return to their traditional export markets," Djunic said.

The EU said it expected the Milosevic government to begin talks with the opposition parties, make more improvements to its media laws, reform its electoral law and judicial system, and make "substantial progress" on the issue of Kosovo.
"In the absence of progress...towards meeting these criteria the decision on granting autonomous trade preferences will be reviewed," the EU statement said.
